utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Indah Susanti standing in for Crispian Smith for approximately the next two weeks for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, it's Aleksandar Aleksic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday you asked if we could give you a response by this afternoon to the Stanisic's 14th of June, so Monday's, motion for leave to amend his Rule 65 ter list. Your Honours, as I speak, of the 41 documents listed, 12 still do not have translations. So we cannot deal with those at all. Your Honours, can I just mention something in passing, yesterday Mr. Zecevic remarked that the search engine for EDS did not always produce the desired results. And can I just say that this is something we've been saying throughout, that our search engines don't, without any sympathy from the Defence at all. And so we trust the Court will not be very impressed by that. The -- a number of the documents which start with the ERN numbers 0360-9, in fact the Defence have already got several documents starting with these ERN numbers from EDS. And so, as I say, it does rather add to our, I suppose it's complaint, that they could have discovered these documents before, had they run proper searches. However, having said all that, of the documents that relate to, effectively, the CSB Sarajevo, which run from 65 ter 922D1 through to 952D1 - in all, 31 documents - we do not object to the addition of the following, and I will read it out slowly so that it's, I hope, on the transcript for Your Honours: 924D1, 925D1, 928D1, 929D1, 933D1, 936D1, 949D1. And so we don't object to the addition to the 65 ter list. We do object to the following because we say they have no relevance at the present that we can see. Some relate to municipalities outside the indictment. Some relate to events that are irrelevant to this case. And those are: 923D1, 926D1, 931D1, 932D1, 934D1, 937D1, 951D1. The further category for which we object are those that, although they could be said to be marginally relevant, are not sufficiently important, which is the test, to be added at this stage: 922D1, 930D1, 935D1, 950D1. Your Honours, 65 ter 927D1 is a list of operatives which was tendered through Mr. Tusevljak yesterday. Now, the version that was tendered, in fact, has a different ERN and has additional handwritten markings on the one, the one that was exhibited yesterday, and so we query whether 927D1 adds anything to the document that was admitted, but we agree that it's relevant. Your Honours, no translations that I said, and I won't bother to read out all the numbers. They're not available for 12 of the documents. Nine documents of these relate to the witness that the Defence have dropped, Mr. Vlaco. They were disclosed by us. They are 65 ter 953D1 to 961D1. We do not object to their addition, however, despite the fact of the witness having been dropped to the 65 ter list. And, Your Honour, the last one was the map of Sarajevo that was drawn, or marked, by Mr. Tusevljak when he was interviewed by the OTP and that's already been admitted. Your Honour, I hope -- that's as helpful as we can be, given, as I say, the lack of translations for the rest. Your Honours, may I also publicly thank Mr. Demirdjian who spent most of this morning going through this rather time-consuming exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we commend the OTP for the effort they put into being able to respond in a timely fashion and indicate their position by classification. So that's all very helpful. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Anything to add, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, perhaps I will have a comment on some of these documents and the classification which was made by the Office of the Prosecutor; however, I wasn't put on notice that Ms. Korner would orally give their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, therefore, I can only give our position on these documents once the documents are brought to me in hard copy. And after the break I can give our position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, good afternoon to you, sir. Before Mr. Zecevic continues his examination-in-chief, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can ask the usher to provide the binder to the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, 1D182, tab 2, was the document that we were dealing with as we were about to break off. Tell me, Mr. Tusevljak ... actually, I think you've answered that question, but let me put it once again: In mid-July did you go to Vogosca to visit the public security station of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion did you speak to the chief of the public security station, and what was the situation that you saw for yourself at the Vogosca Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke to the chief, and the situation we saw there was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because the crime prevention department was not functioning at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat. Can you hear the interpretation now? Could you please repeat your answer because the interpreters did not catch the second part of your answer, the one that had to do with the situation that you found at the public security station of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was chaotic because the crime police was not functioning at all at that station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, yesterday while you were testifying, when you were shown a report that the operatives of the CSB compiled in July, you said that that was the first information that you had received from Vogosca. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the next document, that is tab 67. 65 ter 132D1. This document is dated the 26th of July, 1992, that is to say, after you went to Vogosca. It is signed by the chief of the public security station, Borislav Maksimovic. Do you remember this report of Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was sent to the Ministry of the Interior and it was not sent to the CSB Sarajevo, whereas 69 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zecevic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This first report, 67, was sent to the Ministry of the Interior and then it was probably forwarded to us in Lukavica as well. That's what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tusevljak, before this report do you remember having received any reports from Vogosca apart from this one from the end of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I as the then chief of the crime police department did not receive a single report. That department simply did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of this report on page 1 it is stated that in the months of May, June, and July ten policemen were engaged on the front line. Do you know whether some dispatches arrived at the CSB from Vogosca to other departments before this one at the end of July?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you take it if I don't get up and object, I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D577, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us please have a look at 932D1, tab 173.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a moment ago Ms. Korner said on page 2, line 18, that some of these documents, including this one, do not -- or, rather, are irrelevant for this case and that they have to do with events that are of no relevance to this case. I absolutely disagree, since you will see from the document that this document pertains to Vogosca. That is a municipality that is included in this indictment. And this is an order of the chief to send active, experienced policemen to the territory of the municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, do you see this order in front of you? The date is the 10th of September and it is signed by the chief of the CSB, Zoran Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you recognise Mr. Cvijetic's signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the CSB by way of this order addresses some of these subordinate public security stations and asks them to appoint some active-duty policemen and to assign them to work on certain tasks in Vogosca; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the reason for these policemen, these experienced professional policemen, to be sent by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, there's no -- the words "experienced" do not appear. It asks that they be experienced. It asks in paragraph 2 that they should be experienced. It doesn't say that those who were sent were experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it says clearly in -- at least in Serbian, "the policemen who will be dispatched need to be experienced and qualified."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the future. It doesn't mean to say that's what happened, which is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just talking about the order. This is the order of the chief of the CSB. And clearly, Ms. Korner, chief of the CSB requests that the people who are sent are experienced and qualified policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I confess that I don't understand the basis of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The objection was that what was the reason for these experienced professional policemen to be sent, in other words, it suggested that they be sent. My quarrel was with the way Mr. Zecevic put it. If he simply read out the words that were in the document, in English anyhow, that's one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, do you know whether these policemen from these police stations, the ones that are mentioned here, whether they actually went to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the reason for these policemen with these characteristics to go to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was obvious that the policemen who were working in Vogosca at the police station were not up to the task for which they were there in the first place, that is to say, to establish law and order and to prevent the commission of different crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After this group of policemen went there, a total of 30, I believe, did the situation in the public security station of Vogosca change? Did it improve?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that we received, the situation was considerably improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence. Obviously it is a relevant document. And I don't know whether Ms. Korner intends to withdraw her objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, Your Honour, I don't. No, Your Honour, I don't. For two reasons: Firstly, it hasn't been explained why the police officers went there; it hasn't been explained - I'm just checking - whether the witness actually saw this document at the time and, if so, why; third, he hasn't explained how he knows that these officers were actually sent there. So we say this witness cannot -- unless he can give further evidence about it, allow this document to be admitted. We simply don't know what they were sent there for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But isn't the document on its face relevant, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in what sense? It simply says these officers were sent to Vogosca. If one knew why they were sent there, that would be one matter, but we don't. Your Honour, I have no doubt at all that if one went through, ploughed through, all the documentation, found many examples of officers being transferred from one police station to another. There could have been combat, sickness, anything. We have no idea why. If it's said to be relevant to an issue, then we have to know why they were sent there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think I now understand your objection, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm probably missing something here. The objection -- the objection by Ms. Korner at the beginning of today was that the document 932 is irrelevant because it deals with the events which are outside the scope of the indictment and it's irrelevant for this case. That was her objection. Now we are getting another objection, a different objection. However, however, if I may just quote the transcript, the answer of the witness. My question was: "Q. Mr. Tusevljak, tell me, what was the reason for these policemen with these characteristics to go to Vogosca?" Meaning experienced and qualified policemen. "A. Because it was obvious that the policemen who were working in Vogosca at the police station were not up to the task for which they were there in the first place, that is to say, to establish law and order and to prevent the commission of different crimes. "Q. After this group of policemen went there, a total of 30, I believe, did the situation in the public security station of Vogosca change? Did it improve? "A. According to the information that we received, the situation was considerably improved." Before that, Mr. Tusevljak said: "The chief of the CSB by way of this order addresses some of the subordinate public stations and ask them to appoint some of the" -- no, that's my question. He confirms that. And then, yes, another question: "Q. Mr. Tusevljak, do you know whether these policemen from this police station, the ones that are mentioned here, whether they actually went to Vogosca? "A. Yes." Now, I'm probably, then, missing something, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I -- I know he said yes, but he doesn't explain how -- this document, on the face of it, has absolutely nothing do with him or his department. I've no doubt at all he's happy to agree with any questions that Mr. Zecevic puts to him, but unless he can explain how he knows this, what they were actually sent there to do, Your Honours, we say this document is not admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will happily ask additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, so I wouldn't accidently make a mistake, I will quote Ms. Korner and I will ask you that question. How do you know that these members of the police went to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Sarajevo CSB, we had morning collegium meetings. In addition to the chief of the Security Services Centre, it was attended by the chief of police, myself as the chief of crime prevention police, chief of the administration department, chief of communications, and perhaps some of the other managerial staff. At these morning meetings we discussed the current problems, both at the centre or in the territory of the centre, about which we sometimes received information. As you can see, this document dates from the month of September 1992. And as early as in July, that is to say, almost two months earlier, we noticed problems at that police station. And by this date the problems had not yet been overcome. For that reason, the chief of police and the chief of the centre - and I was also among those consulted, because the crime prevention police, although it had already been set up at the time, had not been producing any results - it was decided to try and select professional staff from these police stations, that is to say, policemen who already had police experience from before the war, and have them try and help their colleagues at the public security station in Vogosca in carrying out their police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And another question asked by Ms. Korner: What was their task once they were sent to Vogosca? What specifically were they supposed to do there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Establishing public law and order, prevention of commission of crimes, and setting up check-points in order to ensure that the life of the citizens would be normal and undisturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they really carried out this task?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they stayed for over a month in Vogosca and they managed to do this and to carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once again I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the light of the evidence now, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D578, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your opinion, or in view of the Sarajevo CSB Birac-Romanija at the time, was responsible or the most responsible for such a situation at the Vogosca Public Security Station [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the then chief of that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any measures taken against the chief of that police station because of the shortcomings in his work, I mean the overall shortcomings?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that disciplinary proceedings were initiated against the chief and commander. A criminal report was filed for some other activities, and they were eventually removed from the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will show you document 1D184, tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 26. 1D184.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 15th of October, 1992. It is signed by the chief of the Security Services Centre. It is a decision on measures of temporary removal from tasks and assignments. Do you remember this decision and the disciplinary proceedings from October 1992 initiated against Borislav Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, as for Mr. Maksimovic and some structures in Vogosca, did they put up any resistance to this decision made by the CSB chief, that is to say, the temporary removal of Mr. Borislav Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that police station did not recognise the centre as someone who was managing them, not yet at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For reference, it is 1D342.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I will show you 1D185. It is tab 70. This is a memo by Borislav Maksimovic. It is dated the 31st of October, 1992, and it tells how at a meeting of the Vogosca Public Security Station it was decided not to accept the change of the Vogosca SJB chief and, at the end, that the policemen issued an ultimatum that they would all leave if there was a removal of the chief who was appointed by the Assembly, and only the Assembly could recall him. Do you know that this was the stand taken by the public security station in Vogosca, its chief, and some political structures from Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As one can see, the document was submitted to the Security Services Centre as well, and we knew that we had a problem, that Mr. Maksimovic did not want to leave the position he was at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Maksimovic -- was he eventually forced to leave the position?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see P627, tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the situation and work of the public security station of Vogosca. It is dated the 12th of November, 1992. Please have a look at this report. It is on the screen in front of you. On the last page, page 4 of the Serbian text in the penultimate paragraph. We'll just wait for the English text to appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English text begins on the previous page, so if we could please show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the centre undertook disciplinary measures against the most responsible employees of the public security station, including the former chief, the chief of the crime prevention service, police commander, and his assistants, and they have all been changed by new personnel. And a criminal report was filed against the SJB chief to the relevant prosecutor's office because of abuse of authority and position. Are you aware of this and is this what you had in mind in one of your previous answers?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, who was this report addressed to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the chief of the Security Services Centre. And probably it was then also forwarded to the Ministry of the Interior. I cannot see that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Ministry of the Interior was informed about the resolution of the problem at the public security station in Vogosca, and which measures were taken against the responsible employees from that public security station? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated, as we have seen, the 12th of November. The document I will show you now, 65 ter 124D1, tab 28, is dated the 13th of November, 1992. Sir, this is a report. And on page 4 it is typed "chief of CSB, Zoran Cvijetic." However, the copy we have here is not signed. Are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an operative report which was confidential at the time, because one can see that it has to do with the TAS action, the theft of vehicles, and what the Sarajevo CSB should do in order to finalise this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who was this report addressed to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you say the minister or the ministry?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry. Such reports we addressed to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a comprehensive report about the issue, the theft of misappropriation of vehicles from the TAS factory? Is it the most comprehensive report that you had at that moment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the exact data which were available to us at the Security Services Centre at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have all the information included in this report before the moment when the report was drafted?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the information collected by us from July 1992 up to and including the moment of writing of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When we speak about the events mentioned in this memo and some other events in the Vogosca municipality, is it possible to say that the managerial staff of the public security station in Vogosca did not exactly want to co-operate in resolving these issues?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until they were replaced by other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, I'm really sorry, but leading -- I did object yesterday, and can I just point out that a leading question like that, "is it possible to say that the managerial staff of the public security station in Vogosca did not exactly want to co-operation," is a thoroughly leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, I have to rephrase this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic does not have to rephrase the question. He's asked the leading question, he got the answer he wanted, and to rephrase the question is absolutely pointless. I'm merely making this objection so it's clear for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no objection, I propose to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no objection. The only query I have is, he said it was addressed to the -- the witness said it was addressed to the Ministry of the Interior. I may be missing something, but I don't see that on the document. If it's right, perhaps the witness could just point out where that is or whether he simply knows as a result of his experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, on the basis of what did you say that this document was sent to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the practice at the time. And this is not the only example of this kind of information. There was a constant information flow towards the ministry about similar events. There should be a cover letter, that is currently not present here, from which it would be possible to see that the document was sent to the ministry. Had it not been sent to the ministry, it wouldn't have been worded in this particular way. It is very comprehensive, it describes the TAS operation, and that was the purpose of the writing of this document and sending it to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who signed this information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, it was signed by the chief of the CSB, Zoran Cvijetic. This means that the purpose of this information was to be sent to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you're satisfied, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said I didn't object. I merely queried how he said it was addressed to the Ministry of the Interior, which, on the face of the document, is not evident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D579, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Trial Chamber's reference: Disciplinary proceedings against Borislav Maksimovic is 1D186.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, were there any other persons in Vogosca against whom disciplinary proceedings were instituted by the chief of the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe disciplinary proceedings were also instituted against the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Tjelovic [as interpreted]. I just read it here. He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Trial Chamber's reference, this is 1D187. That's the document about the disciplinary proceedings against Vlado Tjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minor thing for the transcript: It's Vlado Kelovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, yesterday you testified about the number of public security stations that were subordinated to the Public Security Centre Sarajevo Birac-Romanija. Could you remind us of the number once again?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the moment there were 22 public security stations or police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter, Prosecution document, 10133, tab 146. It's a map of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe you have much smaller version. And on the screen you will be able to see a much larger version. And I would like your comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding is this is an exhibit; it's part of the bundle of maps that we handed over, I think, right at the beginning, simply for the purpose of transcript. I thought we made the whole -- there was a book of maps, as it were, and I thought the whole book had become an exhibit. Because if it wasn't admitted, it ought to have been admitted some time ago. It's been used quite often, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We seem to agree with you that we think it was exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, Your Honours, since I will require a witness to make some markings on the map, it will definitely get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- a new number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- a new number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, with the help of the usher, I would like to ask you to mark, to circle, or whatever you find convenient, I would like you to mark on the screen public security stations that were subordinated to the CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask for one thing: Could we zoom in on the eastern part of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So actually the right side of the map should be enlarged. The lower part. Right there. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that all right? And while you are making the markings, could you also mention the names of the stations.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trnovo, Hadzici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Vogosca, Ilijas, part of the police station in Visoko, Novo Sarajevo, police station in Novi Grad in Sarajevo at the beginning. Pale, Sokolac, Rogatica, Olovo, Bratunac, Skelani, I don't find it on the map but it's somewhere around here. Zvornik, Vlasenica, Sekovici. I think that's about it. Excuse me, Osmaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Milici as well, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the exhibit number for the map with the markings, that is, the names of the places underlined, where the public security stations were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's admitted and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D580, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, you've explained and shown on the map the public security stations that were subordinated to the Security Services Centre Sarajevo Romanija-Birac. Yesterday you were describing the problems that arose in attempting to physically communicate with Vogosca and Ilijas. Did you have similar problems with some other public security stations that you just underlined on the map? I'm talking here about the physical access to those public security stations.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me mention just one more thing: I also forgot the police station Centar and the police station Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They are both in the city of Sarajevo? Part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you now answer my previous question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the communications with all the police stations in the territory of the Birac region was severed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say the Birac region, could you list the stations that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skelani, Bratunac, Zvornik, Milici, Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go one by one. What were the reasons that there was no physical communication with those stations?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications were cut off. The roads that one would normally use to drive there were taken over by the BiH Territorial Defence. This means that the aforementioned places could be reached only via a detour. Skelani and Bratunac could be reached only from the territory of the Republic of Serbia. The other stations could be reached only using a detour via forest roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we slightly move the map to the part of the map that we looked at just a moment ago. One more. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you again show us on this map, or, rather, simply explain the position, the location, of Skelani and Bratunac. You don't have to mark anything; just tell us, where are they? Please explain this briefly so that we shouldn't waste any more time. You can just say whether they are --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are practically on the bank of the Drina River. Both Skelani and Bratunac and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us explain something here. Was it possible to reach Skelani and Bratunac from the territory of the Bosnia and Herzegovina, the former Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the beginning it was impossible to reach those places from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina because all the roads were cut off or taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tusevljak, did you attend the first collegium meeting of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held in Belgrade in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P160.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's number 153 in your binder. Sir, this is a brief analysis of the work to date and basic guide-lines for the future work, meaning a summary of the meeting. The first part of the document contains the brief description of the discussion at the meeting. And from page 20 onwards, we find the conclusions of the collegium. Do you remember whether you took floor on the meeting of this collegium.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did not speak. I think it was only the chief of the centre who spoke at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 18 in Serbian, it says: "Simo Tusevljak, chief of the crime prevention department in the CSB Sarajevo." Could you read that part in order to refresh your memory so I can then ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 18 in Serbian. It's ERN 0324-1868. 1868. Three more pages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's in Serbian. It doesn't help. What is it in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 18 in English as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember now that you spoke at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Having read the brief summary of your words at the meeting, do you remember whether this is a correct summary of what you said on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you spoke at that meeting about the lack of personnel dealing with the crime in the centre itself and in the territory covered by the centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite obvious that I spoke about that because it was our main problem. We didn't have the sufficient number of operatives, of inspectors who were supposed to work on the prevention of crime, and also we did not have the sufficient number of the crime technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 we see that the primary job was documenting war crimes and filing crime reports including cases of war crimes committed by Serbs. Do you remember that you spoke about this topic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We requested the operatives working in public security stations to document all crimes, wherever we had any crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Some information from Vlasenica is being provided here, the total number of criminal reports and the number of criminal reports filed against Serbs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I read it here, I do remember. But it is 73 criminal reports that were filed for all crimes, that is to say, everything that is happening there and everything that the crime police in Vlasenica had done until this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, what is written here, was that really your primary job? This, what is written here in relation to war crimes.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to this work in terms of what we were asking the crime police on the ground to do, I've already said this, our major problem, in general, was the establishment of the crime police as such, and you can see that from my initial remarks, namely that at that point in time there were only two other inspectors working in the CSB alongside myself, that is to say, I and two other men were doing the job of 100 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, did you really document cases of war crimes that were perpetrated by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever the crime police was asked to come to the scene by the investigating judge or anyone else, we did carry out an on-site investigation, we gathered all the evidence, and we submitted it to prosecutor's offices where they existed, and we tried to find the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During 1992, at any point in time - how should I put this? - did you make any kind of distinction in terms of filing criminal reports or investigates crimes, including war crimes, in relation to the ethnic background of the victim or the possible perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All operatives on the basis of the instructions that we had from July and August, and we could only work on the basis of instructions, we asked in all of these instructions that everything be done equally in respect of all of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 20 - and I assume that that is 20 or 21 in English - the conclusions of this meeting of the 11th of July are listed. Three pages ahead in Serbian - and I assume that is the same in English - paragraphs 6 and 7 of the conclusions, can we have a look at that and can we hear your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just been informed that the English starts on page 22 and continues, in part, on page 23 as well. I think it's the next page. So it's 6 and 7. Over here, we see paragraph 4. Can we please have the Serbian text as well, page 26 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, the conclusions are listed here. Number 6 is preventing and documenting war crimes and using all legally-prescribed resources and methods for documenting, et cetera, and filing criminal reports not only against identified perpetrators but also those who are unidentified. Do you remember that this kind of conclusion was reached at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received these minutes and these conclusions, and I was aware of all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you received this, who received it? Was it the CSBs, the public security stations? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the CSB received it. Now, did the chief distribute this further on to the public security stations? I don't know, although I see that these conclusions themselves say that that was supposed to be done. And this was probably sent further on to all the chiefs of the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that this response of yours pertains to conclusion number 7 as well, which follows after the one we've just looked at.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's an integral part as well, number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you remember whether these conclusions were carried out in practice, first of the CSB and then also the public security stations in the area?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the CSB we immediately set out, those of us who were there, to carry out these conclusions. And that is something that was called for at the meetings that followed - at the collegium meetings, and with the chiefs of the crime police, wherever these departments were formed - and they were asked to take these measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak a bit slower for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P610, tab 16. Could that please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this a convenient point to take the break, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, whilst the witness is being returned, can I just say something in respect of the list of documents to which we dealt with this morning. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just for the usher, I need to make submissions, so the witness should be kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the -- the problems, apart from the speed and the lack of translations, was, Your Honours, when we applied to add new documents to our 65 ter list, in terms said we had to give full reasons as to why we wanted to do so and what the relevance was so that Your Honours were able to see why we were making the application for a late addition. Your Honours, one of the problems we had was this; the Defence motion at paragraph 5 said, under subparagraph (a): "Documents 922D1 to 938D1, 941D1 to 944D1, and 946D1 to 952D1 originate from CSB Romanija-Birac. These documents relate to the functioning of the CSB, staffing, communications, implementation of RS MUP orders, problems with paramilitaries, re-subordination to the VRS, disciplinary proceedings, and inspections, which are all live issues in the proceedings." Your Honours, the difficulty is, with that particular document - which when we had an explanation from the witness, I withdrew my objection - on the face of it, it's quite impossible to see why the fact that officers from other police stations had been sent to Visegrad should be deemed to be relevant. Your Honours, we would ask that we get proper descriptions, as we were made to do for the purposes of additions to the 65 ter list, as to why, to what issue, the document is actually relevant. As I say, in a round-up paragraph like that, it was almost impossible to tell. It's only when you get an explanation that we're able to give a reasoned response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely what I intend to do because I was invited by the Trial Chamber to do so after the break. Your. Honours, first, the documents which Ms. Korner objected as based on the fact that according to her they are irrelevant to the case, is document 923D1. 923D1 is a document sent by one of the SJBs to the CSB Sarajevo. One of the SJBs being Bratunac SJB. This is the response to the request by CSB of 18th of July, 1992. It shows the actual problem, which the witness actually testified before, that there was a lack of active-duty policemen and a lack of personnel in the CSB -- in the SJB Bratunac, which is one of the SJBs under the territory of CSB Sarajevo. As the CSB Sarajevo is a part of the indictment and an allegation made by the indictment, and during the Prosecutor's case are that the chief of the CSB and some other members of the CSB were members of the joint criminal enterprise, therefore it's very relevant to see what is the situation in the field, in the territory which covers the CSB. Apart from that, this document is important because it shows that after the 11th of July collegium, certain measures were undertaken to -- to see -- to actually definitely find that the CSBs were required to definitely inform the ministry of the situation in the field and in their SJBs which were subordinated to them. It goes to the information. It goes to the knowledge of the ministry and the accused about the situation in the field. So, therefore, it's very relevant, in my opinion. Document 926D1 is a document again dated 12th December, 1992, so relevant for the indictment. It is SJB Sokolac sent -- dispatch sent to MUP of Republika Srpska in Bijeljina and CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac. And it goes to the issue of re-subordination of the police to the army, because it says clearly "on request of the command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade and the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on this particular date re-subordinated the members of police to the army." Number three is the document 931D1. It is the document dated 31st of August, 1992, signed by Mr. -- late Zoran Cvijetic, the chief of CSB Sarajevo Birac, where he dispatches 12 workers, 12 policemen, to Zvornik for the purposes, and the witness will confirm that the purposes were actually the same one as the other case which we discussed previously, the case of Vogosca. Therefore, it's relevant since Zvornik is in our indictment. The next document is a document 932, and that is the one we discussed and it was admitted earlier today. The next document is 934D1. This is the document sent by SJB Zvornik dated 18th of October, 1992, signed by the chief of the SJB, sent to the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, the police department in Bijeljina, the CSB Bijeljina, and the CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac. What the purpose of this document is that towards the end of the document the -- the chief of the SJB informs the CSBs and the ministry that he is conducting disciplinary action against one of the policemen. And as Your Honours are aware, that is a live issue in this case. The next document is document 937D1. This is again a document sent by late Zoran Cvijetic, the chief of the CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac, dated 25th of October, 1992, sent to the subordinate SJBs. And this document is about the obligation of the police to -- to secure the convoy, the UNPROFOR convoy, which is going from Belgrade to Sarajevo with the humanitarian aid. The reason why this document is relevant, in our opinion, is that there has been -- during the Prosecutor's case there has been a number of points where Office of the Prosecutor alleged that the securing of the convoys was not the part of the obligation of the Ministry of Interior in accordance with the law and that that shows their criminal intent. Now, and the last document, which allegedly, according to the Prosecution, is relevant to the case, is document 951D1 and this is the document dated 13 November 1992, sent to CSB Sarajevo and to -- and through CSB Sarajevo to SJB Skelani. And Assistant Minister Mr. Tomislav Kovac advises the CSB that the ministry will be sending one of the inspectors to Skelani for the instructive ... inspection, yes, I'm sorry. Instructive inspection. And therefore I believe, to this end, is a relevant document. Now, the second group of documents are the documents which the Office of the Prosecution say is -- are marginally relevant or not sufficiently important. The first document is document 65 ter 922D1. 922D1. It is the document sent from SJB Zvornik. Date of the document, it's 22nd August 1992, to CSB Sarajevo, about the actual composition of the -- and the personnel issues in the SJB Zvornik. SJB Zvornik, as you know, is a part of the indictment. And furthermore -- furthermore, there has been -- on a number of occasions there has been some question from the Office of the Prosecutor to various witnesses about the fact that SJB Zvornik at the beginning was reporting to CSB Bijeljina and there was -- and information or order by Mr. -- by accused Minister Stanisic that the Zvornik is actually a part of the CSB Sarajevo. And this document, sent from SJB Zvornik to CSB Sarajevo, confirms that. And this witness will actually comment on this document. The second document is 930D1. It is, again, the document from CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac, dated 28 August 1992, signed by chief of the CSB, late Zoran Cvijetic, and it's sent to all -- sent to all SJBs subordinated to the CSB. It really struck me that Ms. Korner said this is marginally relevant or not sufficiently important because this document actually talks about the instruction on disciplinary responsibility of the workers of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. And with this document the actual instruction which is already an exhibit in this case was sent to -- by the chief of the CSB to all SJBs in the territory. The next document is 935. 935D1. It is a document dated 24th of October, 1992, signed by chief of the CSB Zoran Cvijetic, and it's sent to all the SJBs in the territory. And this is actually a document by which the CSB chief is forwarding the order of minister of interior dated 23rd of October, 1992. So it shows that at that point in time these orders by the minister were -- were sent down the line to the SJBs. And the last document is the document which is allegedly irrelevant or -- I'm sorry, it's not that, it's marginally relevant or not sufficiently important. It's the document 950D1. And this document is sent by SJB Vogosca. We assume it was sent to the CSB Sarajevo, although it doesn't say so, but the witness will be able to comment on that. This document is relevant because of two things: First thing is that SJB Vogosca is a municipality in our indictment; and the second ... and the second point of relevancy is, again, re-subordination of the police units to the army, because at the very end it says all -- it is informing about the number of the policemen who were killed in combat or wounded in combat, and it says at the very end that all these policemen -- all these members of the Ministry of Interior on the order of the command of the Vogosca Brigade were engaged in defending the first line because of the heavy attacks on our -- on their positions. So, therefore, we believe that all these documents, for the reasons I just stated, are relevant and that are for these reasons the objection by the Office of the Prosecutor is not -- doesn't have merit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've just wasted 20 minutes on something that should have been said in the original motion and might have produced a different response from us. And I reiterate the position that Your Honours place the Prosecution in, which should have been adhered to by the Defence. Your Honours, as I said yesterday, I knew that most of these documents were probably going to be shown to the witness and could have been dealt with on a case-by-case basis. However, I should say this: The -- as Your Honours will see, it's confirmed a number of these documents do not relate to either municipalities that are within the indictment or matters that are within the indictment either. But, Your Honour, can I just reiterate about disciplinary proceedings; I cannot think how many times we have said this, and the Defence persist: We do not dispute there were disciplinary procedures. We do not dispute that disciplinary action was taken against members of the MUP. Our case is, no disciplinary action was taken in respect of members of the MUP who committed crimes against non-Serbs. Or - I say "no" - very little, if any. And that's the issue. It is not an issue - and Mr. Zecevic's sarcasm about us saying it was irrelevant is misguided and misplaced - that there were disciplinary procedures. And the rest, as it's all been gone through, as I say, Your Honours, it is probably better to deal with it on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps it is a thing that Ms. Korner was not present. I think we discussed this issue about the disciplinary proceedings and I provided an explanation why this is important, and Your Honours, if you remember, accepted my explanation as relevant for the Defence case. And based on that, one of the documents was admitted into evidence precisely because the knowledge, it goes to the knowledge of the minister, that the disciplinary system exists as such in the territory in 1992. And that is precisely the reason why we are offering these documents, to show that as far as minister is concerned, because he is the one who has to decide and the initiation of the -- or the disciplinary proceedings comes from the chief of the CSB, therefore, if the minister is aware that the disciplinary proceedings are taken or disciplinary measures are taken by the chief of the CSB, I think that that is an important element in the overall view of the situation at the time and for Your Honours' decision on that particular issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was aware of that. It doesn't change the position. Indeed, Your Honours had declined the Defence application to admit a number of disciplinary actions before. It is not in dispute; we know that the minister signed off on appeals on disciplinary action. If Your Honours are prepared to have documents in that take this case absolutely no further, that, of course, is a matter for Your Honours. We took the view that Your Honours were reluctant to admit documents unless they add real value to the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we have the witness back to the stand. We would rule on this matter in the course of -- before we rise for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, before the break we discussed the document that includes the conclusions of the first collegium meeting held on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have a look at P610, tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before we start commenting on this document, could you please have a look at the document that we looked at previously. Conclusions. That is tab 153. And could you please tell me, then, in your view, how many conclusions are there? It's on the last page, the number of conclusions.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eighteen conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to this document, number P610, tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, there is no date here. There is a reference to August 1992. And it says "Report on the implementation of conclusions from the meeting of senior MUP personnel held on the 11th of July, 1992." The document is not signed. Can you tell us whether you are familiar with this report, and can you tell us who this report was sent to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report that was also written for the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what do you conclude that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the first page where it says that this is a strictly confidential report. If the CSB -- and we see in the letterhead that it's the Serb Republic, Ministry of the Interior, Romanija-Birac CSB, there is no reference to any department here, say the department of the crime police, that means the chief of the CSB or his service are writing this report, and this is being written in order to respond to some request that had been made by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many points or items does this report have altogether?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that it is 18 altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're done with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, can we please look at 928D1, tab 151. This is a document that states the date of the 18th of July, 1992. It Says "Public Announcement." Romanija-Birac CSB. Can you tell us what this is? What is this document? Are you familiar with it, and what was the reason for writing up this kind of document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a public announcement or a press release dated the 18th of July, 1992. Actually, the media were in Pale at the time and they were covering the CSB and citizens were being called upon -- since it became obvious that crime was on the rise, the police was publicly calling upon citizens to stop doing that kind of thing because the police were not able to do their regular work, as they were defending the country. So this is a press release written up by the chief or someone from his office, and this was actually released to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What does this press release say? Persons who do not act in accordance with this document or in accordance with the law, are there going to be consequences?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is obvious. You can see it from the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why was it possible for these kind of public announcements to be made and released through the media?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the assessment then was, with the members of the military of Republika Srpska as well, that all such things should be brought to an end and that more energetic measures should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is the month of July, these energetic measures, as you said, and also bringing this kind of conduct to an end, why was all of that not done before that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a simple reason, as I've already said: We did not have enough people. Also, the number of people I had, say, in the crime police and in the police itself, a huge number were involved in combat and they were not able to be involved in police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, you know, Your Honours, it's a matter for you, really, I mean, if you think it's relevant. I cannot see any strong objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D581, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we please now have tab 3. That's P589.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 25th of July, 1992. It is signed by chief of the Security Services Centre, Zoran Cvijetic. And it is addressed, as we can see, to the Ministry of the Interior, Sarajevo, and it refers to a memo which was received from the ministry on the 19th of July, 1992, obviously. Do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph on the first page, the report says that the problems are present because of insufficient number of men and this refers to the crime prevention service, which you were managing at the time. Do you remember that this was the specific problem?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Throughout this time, our greatest problem was a lack of adequately-trained workers, that is to say, inspectors who knew how to discharge the duties of crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the second sentence here talks about problems with preparing data due to war operations, poor communication, and so on. You have explained to us what was the territory covered by the Security Services Centre, and you confirmed in your previous testimony what problems existed in terms of physical communication. Please tell me, did you have any other way to communicate with public security stations and to what extent was that operational?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A communications centre of the Security Services Centre was set up; however, that communications centre very often could not meet our needs. That is to say, the dispatches or the memos which were sent by the Security Services Centre could not be sent. And then we looked for other means such as sending couriers or in some other ways when communication was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And these alternative ways of communication, how did they reflect on the ability to receive information in a timely fashion or send instructions to the field?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document itself shows that very often, precisely because it was impossible to send requests or because we did not receive answers in due time, we could not meet the dead-lines which we received in dispatches and documents from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tusevljak, please tell me whether at the Security Services Centre level during 1992 you held meetings with managerial staff from public security stations on the basis of their lines of work?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the first meeting of the kind was only held in July or perhaps August 1992. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will show you the document 1D328, which is tab 6. This is a report on the meeting of the managerial staff in charge of crime prevention from the territory of the Romanija-Birac CSB. And at the beginning it says that on the 27th of July, 1992, in Sokolac a meeting was held. Are you familiar with this document and its subject?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report from that working meeting which we organised on the 27th of July in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What meeting was that? You said awhile ago that you held the first meeting with managerial staff in July or August. Was that this meeting or was that another meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was this meeting. So the conclusion is that this is the first meeting we held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is a summary here, the summary of what those who participated in the discussion at the meeting said. It is mentioned here that you opened the meeting and then it is outlined what you said at the meeting. Can you please read that and tell me whether that more or less reflects what you talked about on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wish to point out that one can see from this report that representatives of the crime police from Vogosca and Rajlovac did not attend the meeting, though they were invited. That was the month of July when we requested that they should begin working. And I can read from the report that I said that in the war conditions crime services in all their segments act under specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, sir, please, there is no need for you to read it out. The document speaks for itself and it is already an exhibit. I'm just interested in hearing from you whether it reflects what you talked about at the time and then I will ask you a specific question so that we can shorten the time needed for this.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So does this document accurately reflect what you said on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please comment on what we can find on page 1 in the sentence where you say: "Due to difficulties in communication, he suggested that within the CSB a mini-regionalisation should be done in such a way to compose three regions," and then there is the first, the second, and the third regions. "The purpose of this regionalisation is improvement of coordination between different" and so on and so forth. Can you give us an explanation and tell us why you proposed this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because it was my assessment at the time that the work of crime police departments would be significantly improved if we managed to make this mini-re-organisation because it was impossible to keep communicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The interpreters haven't heard you or didn't understand what you wanted to say so can you please explain that and give us your answer slowly.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to difficulties in communication and because it was not possible to have communication between the various departments, I proposed this mini-re-organisation so that operatives or heads of crime prevention service in the area could discharge their tasks and duties as successfully as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the meeting was also attended by some employees of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska? From the seat of the ministry, I mean.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that the chief of the crime prevention service Goran Macar attended the meeting, and I think that he was also with Nikola Milanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat what was the position of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 3 of this document in the Serbian version -- can you please repeat what was the position of Mr. Nikola Milanovic in MUP because this has not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an inspector at the crime police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3 it is noted that there was a discussion by Predrag Lucic who was the chief of the crime prevention service in Han Pijesak, who talked about the problem of official communication which made it difficult to work on crime prevention cases. He also said that his service had 40 completed files on criminal acts but they did not have anyone to submit them to because the office of the prosecutor had not been established in the area as yet. Please tell me, this problem of the existence, or, rather, the non-existence of the judicial organs at the time in the territory of the Security Services Centre, the one that was covered by the CSB, was it a big problem, and how big was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The non-existence of courts and prosecutors' offices in our area was one of the major problems because, as you can see, in the month of July in many areas there was no one that we could file the criminal reports or official reports with because neither a court or a prosecutor's office existed. If we knew who the perpetrator of a crime was, there was no one to hand him over to. We had no prosecutor. We had no investigating judge. And that represented a major problem for our work. The problem was that on the territory of the city of Sarajevo there were two basic courts and there was also the higher court in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it existed, when did it exist? Can you just specify that. Which period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period before the 4th of April, 1992. The seat of these courts remained in the territory which was under the control of the Bosnian Muslims. Which means that in the city, territories which were under the control of the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska, these judicial institutions or the seats of these institutions did not exist at all, and we needed to set them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In such instances if there was no one to submit a criminal report with, what did you do with documents? Or if a criminal report had been written, what did you do with it? In such cases, what was done?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We waited for a prosecutor's office and court to be set up. And once they were established, all these reports were handed over to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that just the way in which you worked at the Security Services Centre or was there an instruction for public security stations to do the same if the judicial organs in their area had not been established as yet?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible for them to do this in any other way because who can you submit a report to if there is no court and no prosecutor's office in your area?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was the percentage of the stations or even what was the number of stations, if you know, or how many places were there in which public security stations existed, and in which judicial organs also existed; and on the contrary, in how many places were such institutions non-existent throughout 1992, or at least until some point in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that in the month of April, and perhaps even in May, in perhaps 100 per cent of the territory the judicial organs did not exist, and then they began to be set up on a monthly basis. I think that it was only in late fall that the whole territory was covered. So by the fall about 80 per cent of these stations were not able to submit criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Zecevic wanted the question answered, because it wasn't answered. He asked at page 44, line 9: "Was that just the way in which you worked at the security services centre or was there an instruction for public security stations to do the same ...?" And the answer came back, It wasn't possible for them to do them in any other way. And the actual question wasn't answered. I don't know if Mr. Zecevic wants it answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an issue of interpretation. The question was whether the crime reports and the whole files were set aside waiting for the judicial organs to be established. Was this the practice only in the public security service or were all public security stations in the territory supposed to follow the same practice?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no official instruction on this. In the Security Services Centre in this period, it was only I and two inspectors who worked on this, which meant that we did not file a single criminal report. Public security stations in the field had to rely on their own resources and ingenuity. They did what they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what it means, "they did what they could"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those places where a court and prosecutor's office had been established, crime reports were submitted. And where those organs had not been established, crime reports were not submitted. They waited until the moment that judicial organs would be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now that we've touched upon this issue, Mr. Tusevljak, do you know what a KU register is?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a register of criminal reports. This means that when the crime prevention service completes a file, they submit a criminal report against a known or unknown perpetrator. Such a report is submitted to a prosecutor's office. On this occasion, basic elements of the file are recorded in the crime register, KU register: usually, the kind of the offence; whether the perpetrator is known or unknown; the identity of the perpetrator, if known; and to which basic or district prosecutor's office the crime report was submitted.
